past_medical_history: Primary biliary cholangitis (PBC), end-stage liver disease, Child-Pugh B
family_history: No relevant family history of neuromuscular disease

neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert and oriented. Mildly encephalopathic at baseline (known hepatic encephalopathy grade 1).
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Intact. No facial weakness. No ophthalmoplegia. Gag preserved.
neurological_exam.motor: Proximal lower extremity weakness: hip flexion 3/5 bilaterally, knee extension 3+/5. Upper extremity proximal strength 4/5. Distal strength 4+/5.
neurological_exam.sensory: Intact light touch and pinprick throughout.
neurological_exam.reflexes: Absent bilateral patellar and Achilles. Trace bilateral biceps. Downgoing plantars.
neurological_exam.coordination: Intact finger-nose bilaterally. Limited heel-shin assessment.
neurological_exam.gait: Unable to assess — patient cannot stand.
neurological_exam.additional: FVC: 1.8 L (predicted 2.9 L — 62%). NIF: -28 cmH2O. Serum CK markedly elevated on admission. Proximal > distal weakness pattern. History of 6 weeks of progressive weakness, with onset following bronchitis.

patient.chief_complaint: Six-week progressive weakness predominantly proximal lower extremities, preceded by bronchitis, with absent knee and ankle reflexes.
patient.history_present_illness: Ms. V. is a 54-year-old woman with end-stage liver disease secondary to primary biliary cholangitis, type 2 diabetes, hypertension, and remote splenectomy presenting with a 6-week history of progressive weakness. She had an episode of bronchitis approximately 7 weeks ago requiring a short course of antibiotics. One week after the bronchitis resolved, she began noticing difficulty rising from a chair and climbing stairs. The weakness has been primarily proximal and lower extremity-predominant. She denies any sensory symptoms, pain, or difficulty with sphincters. She has no diplopia or dysphagia. She denies alcohol use. Her atorvastatin was continued throughout. Her husband noted she seemed more confused than her baseline mild hepatic encephalopathy, though ammonia is not significantly elevated. The 6-week duration of proximal weakness, together with the statin use, liver disease, and elevated muscle enzymes, raised initial concern for an inflammatory or statin-induced myopathy or a chronic demyelinating polyneuropathy.

labs.interpretation: Abnormal values: WBC 11.4 x10^9/L (H), Hemoglobin 10.8 g/dL (L), Platelets 88 x10^9/L (L), Total Bilirubin 3.2 mg/dL (H), ALP 428 U/L (H), ALT 62 U/L (H), INR 1.9 (H), Creatine Kinase (CK) 642 U/L (H), Myoglobin 580 µg/L (H), Anti-mitochondrial antibody (AMA) Positive (M2 subtype, high titer) (H), Ammonia 68 µmol/L (H).

findings.finding: DML 7.6 ms (prolonged); CV 30 m/s (reduced); CMAP 2.2 mV (reduced)
DML 6.8 ms; CV 32 m/s (reduced); CMAP 2.8 mV
Absent bilateral peroneal; prolonged median 56 ms
Increased polyphasic units, reduced recruitment in lower extremity muscles consistent with neurogenic changes. Short-duration polyphasic units in proximal muscles.

quantitative_data.pattern: Mixed demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy with concurrent myopathic features on EMG

specialized_test.impression: This is an ABNORMAL nerve conduction study. 1. Prolonged distal motor latencies and reduced conduction velocities in bilateral peroneal and tibial motor nerves, with reduced CMAP amplitudes; borderline changes in median motor nerves. 2. Absent sural sensory nerve action potentials bilaterally. 3. Absent F-waves bilaterally (peroneal); prolonged F-wave latency in bilateral median nerves (56 ms). 4. Absent H-reflex bilaterally. 5. EMG: neurogenic motor unit changes in lower extremity muscles; short-duration polyphasic units in proximal muscles also noted. Demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy with proximal involvement. Mixed neurogenic and possible myopathic EMG features

ecg.interpretation: Sinus tachycardia, rate 98. Borderline QTc prolongation (452 ms). No acute ST-T wave changes.

cardiac_monitoring.rhythm_summary: Sinus rhythm with recurrent sinus bradycardia to 42 bpm and two sinus pauses of 3.2 and 3.8 seconds, both during tracheal suctioning; alternating sinus tachycardia to 138 bpm

events.description: During tracheal suctioning; asymptomatic, resolved spontaneously
During suctioning; prompted atropine at the bedside and continued ICU monitoring
Systolic swings from 178 to 96 mmHg without postural change

findings: Recurrent sinus bradycardia with pauses greater than 3 seconds
Blood-pressure lability without a postural trigger
No sustained tachyarrhythmia and no AV block
cardiac_monitoring.impression: Continuous inpatient telemetry through the period of maximal weakness. Autonomic instability is present in about two thirds of patients with Guillain-Barré syndrome and is a leading cause of in-hospital death, so this recording is a monitoring requirement rather than a diagnostic test: it detects the bradyarrhythmias, pauses and blood-pressure lability that trigger ICU escalation, alongside serial respiratory function. Pauses beyond 3 seconds with blood-pressure lability constitute significant dysautonomia: continuous monitoring is maintained, atropine kept at the bedside, and suctioning treated as a provocative manoeuvre.

output.appearance: Xanthochromic (yellow-tinged) — hepatic jaundice affecting CSF pigmentation
output.interpretation: Opening pressure: 148 mmH2O (normal). Nucleated cell count: 4 cells/mm3. Protein: 96 mg/dL (elevated). Glucose: 58 mg/dL (CSF:serum ratio 0.64). Gram stain: No organisms. Culture: No growth. Note: xanthochromia present (yellow-tinged appearance). Elevated protein with near-normal cell count — a pattern of albuminocytologic dissociation

output.rhythm_summary: Mild sinus tachycardia. No significant arrhythmias.
output.impression: 96-hour continuous telemetry. Mild sinus tachycardia throughout (range 62–110 bpm). Transient tachycardia to 110 bpm on one occasion. No sustained arrhythmia or significant conduction abnormality recorded

output.proposed: IVIG 0.4 g/kg/day x 5 days in patient with PBC/end-stage liver disease
interactions: IVIG in liver disease: sucrose-based IVIG may worsen renal impairment — use non-sucrose formulation (e.g., flebogamma or gammagard liquid)
contraindications: IgA deficiency should be screened before IVIG — check serum IgA
warnings: INR 1.9 — ensure FFP correction before LP; IVIG infusion itself does not require clotting factor correction
Metformin: hold if contrast or renal stress anticipated
Spironolactone: monitor electrolytes closely during IVIG infusion
alternatives: Plasmapheresis: relative contraindication with coagulopathy and thrombocytopenia — IVIG preferred in this patient

quantitative_data.enhancement_pattern: Moderate nerve root enhancement consistent with inflammatory polyradiculopathy

output.impression: 1. Moderate gadolinium enhancement of bilateral lumbosacral nerve roots. 2. No intrinsic spinal cord signal abnormality. 3. Mild degenerative disc changes L4–L5 without canal stenosis. Nerve root enhancement consistent with an inflammatory polyradiculopathy

background.sleep_features: normal vertex waves and sleep spindles

general.summary: No directly applicable, high-quality evidence was retrieved for this query. Recommend correlating with current society guidelines.

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Guillain-Barré syndrome, AIDP (post-bronchitis), with concurrent PBC-associated immunologic background

differential.key_features: Primary biliary cholangitis can be associated with cryoglobulinaemia and vasculitic neuropathy — typically asymmetric mononeuropathy multiplex, not symmetric ascending areflexic weakness.
Time course at presentation is too short to discriminate; revisit beyond 8 weeks.
Encephalopathic features absent; bilirubin / ammonia not consistent.
UDCA is not a recognised cause of acute polyradiculoneuropathy.

optimal_actions.action: Obtain CBC, CMP, HIV, anti-GM1/anti-GQ1b ganglioside antibodies, and stool culture / Campylobacter serology if recent diarrhea
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Mild leukocytosis / elevated inflammatory markers reflecting antecedent infection; ganglioside antibodies for variant typing; trigger identification (Campylobacter, CMV, EBV, Mycoplasma, HIV)

optimal_actions.action: Order nerve conduction studies and needle EMG (EMG/NCS)
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Demyelinating pattern (prolonged DML, conduction block, reduced CV, absent F-waves) consistent with AIDP, or reduced CMAP amplitudes in axonal variants (AMAN/AMSAN)

optimal_actions.action: Perform lumbar puncture for CSF analysis
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Albuminocytologic dissociation — elevated protein with cell count <10/μL; may be normal in the first week of illness

optimal_actions.action: Order bedside respiratory function testing (FVC, MIP/MEP, NIF) and repeat every 4–6 hours
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Baseline and serial FVC, MIP/MEP, NIF; deterioration to FVC <20 mL/kg, MIP worse than -30 cmH2O, or VC <40% predicted triggers ICU transfer / intubation

optimal_actions.action: Search the medical literature for IVIG vs plasma exchange evidence to guide disease-modifying therapy
optimal_actions.expected_finding: IVIG (0.4 g/kg/day x 5 days) and plasma exchange are equivalently effective first-line therapies; combination not superior

optimal_actions.action: Check drug interactions / contraindications for IVIG (renal function, IgA deficiency screen) and/or plasma exchange (coagulation, calcium, hemodynamics)
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Confirmation that IVIG can be given safely (no severe renal impairment, no IgA deficiency) or that plasma exchange is appropriate (adequate vascular access, stable coagulation)

optimal_actions.action: Obtain a 12-lead ECG to screen for autonomic dysrhythmias and baseline QTc
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Sinus tachycardia or bradycardia; conduction or repolarisation abnormalities reflecting autonomic involvement

optimal_actions.action: Start continuous inpatient cardiac telemetry for the period of maximal weakness and keep it running alongside serial respiratory function. Autonomic instability affects about two thirds of patients and is a leading cause of in-hospital death: bradyarrhythmias, pauses beyond 3 seconds and blood-pressure lability are what trigger ICU escalation
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Documentation of sinus pauses, bradyarrhythmias, BP lability, or non-sustained tachyarrhythmias

useless_tools.rationale: GBS is a peripheral nerve / nerve-root disorder; EEG has no role in diagnosis unless atypical CNS features (encephalopathy, seizures) are present.
Echocardiography is not indicated in typical GBS; reserve for pre-existing cardiac disease or unexplained hemodynamic instability after autonomic causes are excluded.
Head CT contributes no diagnostic information in GBS; the disease is peripheral and CT does not visualise nerve roots reliably.
Brain MRI is reserved for atypical features (encephalopathy, CNS signs, transverse myelitis on differential). In classic GBS it does not aid diagnosis.

sequence_constraints.reason: Document respiratory status (FVC/NIF) before committing to IVIG vs plasma exchange — severe respiratory compromise mandates ICU triage and may influence treatment choice and timing.
Renal function, IgA screen, and CBC must be reviewed before IVIG to mitigate renal failure, anaphylaxis (IgA-deficient patients), and aseptic meningitis risk.

critical_actions: Initiate IVIG 0.4 g/kg/day for 5 days; verify hepatic synthetic function (coagulation, albumin) prior to treatment.
Document baseline liver function and avoid hepatotoxic adjuncts.
Coordinate care with hepatology for PBC comanagement.
contraindicated_actions: Do not give corticosteroids as monotherapy in GBS.
Do not start plasma exchange without considering coagulation status given PBC.
key_reasoning_points: Coexisting autoimmune liver disease may complicate workup but does not change the GBS diagnostic threshold.
Vasculitic neuropathy associated with autoimmune comorbidities is typically asymmetric, distinguishing it from symmetric GBS.
Treatment choice between IVIG and PLEX should incorporate hepatic synthetic and coagulation status.

red_herrings.intended_effect: Anchor on a vasculitic or autoimmune neuropathy specific to PBC.
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: PBC-associated neuropathy is typically asymmetric and chronic; the symmetric, ascending, areflexic, albuminocytologic-dissociation profile is GBS.

Agents calling order_specialized_test{respiratory_function} will hit the EMG/NCS output instead.
